    In this work, we study sparse recovery with ℓ∞ error guarantees, a formulation motivated by
variable selection, where the goal is to recover the support of a k-sparse signal in Rd . Our main
contribution is a sharp separation between the oblivious and adaptive models of ℓ∞ sparse recovery.

N (0, 1/n) entries, and let (θ ⋆ , ξ) ∈ Rd × Rn be unknown with nnz(θ ⋆ ) ≤ k. Given observa-
tions y = Xθ ⋆ + ξ, the goal is to output θ ∈ Rd such that nnz(θ) ≤ k and, for a universal
constant C > 0,

Model 1 (Oblivious model) The pair (θ ⋆ , ξ) is chosen independently of X.

Model 2 (Adaptive model) No independence assumption is imposed between (θ ⋆ , ξ) and X.

    Our results show that these two models have fundamentally different sample complexities. In
the oblivious model, the optimal ℓ∞ guarantee is attainable with n ≈ k log d samples and nearly-
linear running time. In particular, when ξ ∼ N (0, σ 2 In ), this gives O(σ)

Theorem 1 Let n = Ω(k log d). There exists a nearly-linear-time estimator which solves Prob-
lem 1 under Model 1, with high probability.

   We further show that the adaptive model exhibits a different behavior: the required sample
complexity is quadratic in k. We give matching upper and lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

Theorem 2 Let n = Ω k 2 log kd . There exists a nearly-linear-time estimator which solves Prob-
                                 

lem 1 under Model 2, with high probability. Conversely, if n = o(k 2 ), then no algorithm can solve
Problem 1 under Model 2 with probability greater than 1/2.

   Thus, up to logarithmic factors, Theorem 2 characterizes both the statistical and computational
complexity of adaptive ℓ∞ sparse recovery. This establishes, to our knowledge, the first separation
between oblivious and adaptive sparse recovery in the ℓ∞ sense. In the standard ℓ2 setting, no such
quadratic separation occurs, and n ≈ k log d samples suffice even in adaptive formulations.1
      Keywords: sparse recovery, variable selection, high-dimensional statistics
